title: I Just Inherited $200,000 Thinking the Step-Up Basis Would Cover My Taxes. Here’s What It Doesn’t Do.
summary: A step-up in basis can reduce capital gains taxes on appreciation that happened before the owner died, but not all inherited assets qualify.
body_markdown:
Inheriting $200,000 does not necessarily mean you will owe taxes on the full amount. Some inherited assets receive a[step-up in basis](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/stepped-up-basis) , which can reduce or eliminate[capital gains taxes](https://smartasset.com/investing/capital-gains-tax-calculator) on growth before the owner died. This does not mean, however, that you are exempt from taxes. You could still get taxed on gains after inheriting.


## What the Step-Up in Basis Covers and Leaves Out


Inherited stocks, real estate and other property generally receive a new basis tied to their[fair market value](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/fair-market-value) on the date of death. This resets your starting point for calculating future gains or losses.


To show how the step-up in basis works, let’s break down a stock inheritance of $200,000. If your parent bought the stock for $80,000 and it is worth $200,000 when you inherit it, the step-up will generally reset the basis to $200,000. So, the $120,000 gain during your parent’s lifetime would not be subject to capital gains tax if you sold the stock at its inherited value.


This is the part of the step-up in basis that many people know, but here is what it does not cover:


Example Does Step-Up Cover It? Why or Why Not


You sell inherited stock for $220,000 (gained $20,000 after inheritance) No Only pre-death gains are eliminated. Your $20,000 post-death gain is still taxable.


[Inherited traditional IRA](https://smartasset.com/retirement/inherited-ira-rules-traditional-roth) with $200,000 in pre-tax contributions No IRAs do not receive a step-up. Distributions remain subject to income tax.


[Inherited real estate](https://smartasset.com/taxes/capital-gains-on-inherited-property) that generates rental income before you sell No Income produced by inherited assets is taxable to you as it accrues.


Inherited rental property that was depreciated before death Generally no separate recapture of the decedent’s prior depreciation solely because you inherited it The inherited property generally receives a new basis at death, which resets the basis used for future depreciation and gain calculations.


Inherited[municipal bonds](https://smartasset.com/investing/all-about-municipal-bonds) earning tax-free interest No The basis adjustment affects gain or loss on the bonds, while qualifying municipal-bond interest generally remains federally tax-exempt.

## Taxes You Could Owe After Inheriting $200,000


The step-up draws a line at the inherited value, but new gains after that point can still create taxes. For example, if the stock goes up from $200,000 to $230,000 before you sell it, your capital gain would be $30,000.


Inherited capital assets are generally treated as[long-term for capital gains](https://smartasset.com/investing/capital-gains-tax-definition) purposes, regardless of how long you hold them.1 The $30,000 gain can be taxed at different rates, depending on your taxable income and filing status.


For 2026, a single filer pays 0% on long-term capital gains when taxable income is $49,450 or less, 15% when taxable income is more than $49,450 but no more than $545,500 and 20% to the extent taxable income exceeds $545,500.2 So, if your[taxable income](https://smartasset.com/taxes/what-is-taxable-income) before the $30,000 already puts the entire gain within one of those ranges, here’s what you could owe:


Example 2026 Long-Term Capital Gains Rate Tax on $30,000 Gain


Single filer with $15,000 in taxable income before the gain 0% $0


Single filer with $100,000 in taxable income before the gain 15% $4,500


Single filer with $550,000 in taxable income before the gain 20% $6,000


At $15,000 in taxable income, the $30,000 gain stays within the 0% range, so no federal capital gains tax would be due. At $100,000, the gain falls within the 15% range, which would mean a $4,500 federal capital gains tax. At $550,000, the gain is taxed at 20%, for a $6,000 federal capital gains tax.

## Know What You Inherited Before You Sell


Before selling inherited assets, identify how each one is taxed. Stocks and real estate generally receive a stepped-up basis, while[traditional IRAs and pretax 401(k)s](https://smartasset.com/retirement/ira-vs-401k) do not get a comparable reset. Keep records showing the date-of-death value on property with a step-up because this amount becomes the starting point used to calculate future gains.


Income generated after the inheritance can create separate tax obligations. This may include dividends, rental income and taxable distributions from inherited retirement accounts. A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_inheritance&utm_content=inherited200kthinkingstepupbasiswouldcovertaxeshereiswhatItdoesnotdo_a) could help you create a plan to manage taxes on inherited assets.
